notes.b: Lipids (fats and oils) reach our diet from three kinds of source: animal, vegetable and marine. Animal sources come from the meat, milk and eggs of land animals, and some are fat in its almost pure form.
points: Meat fat is a major source of lipid in meat products. It includes the visible fat on bacon, the fat trimmed from beef and the fat in sausages. Fatty cuts of lamb and pork, burgers and pâtés also contain it.
Marbling, the fine streaks of fat running inside the muscle of meat, is hidden fat, so a cut can look lean and still contain fat that cannot be trimmed off.
Butter, cream, whole milk, cheese and ice cream supply fat. Milk fat also carries the fat-soluble vitamins A and D, meaning vitamins that dissolve in fat rather than water.
Egg yolk contains fat and lecithin (a fat-like substance that helps fat and water mix). The egg white contains no fat.
Lard is rendered pig fat, which means fat melted down and strained, and is used in pastry and frying.
Suet is the hard fat from around the kidneys and loins of cattle and sheep, used in suet pastry and puddings.
Dripping is the fat that collects from roasted meat, used for frying and roasting.

Visible fat can be seen and cut off or avoided, such as the fat on meat, butter, cooking oil and spreads. Hidden fat is built into foods such as cakes, pastries, biscuits, chocolate, crisps, fried foods, sausages, cheese, ready meals and takeaways.
notes.tip: The fat in an egg is in the yolk, not the white, so name the yolk if asked. Butter belongs here as an animal fat, and the vitamin A in it needs one phrase at most. Cutting fat intake means knowing high-fat foods and lean swaps: trim visible fat, choose lean meat and low-fat dairy, and avoid fried and processed foods.

notes.b: Plants store fat in their fruits, seeds and nuts, and people press this fat out as oil or process it into spreads. Vegetable (plant) sources are the group most often named in exam answers alongside animal and marine.
points: Vegetable oils include olive, sunflower, corn, soya, rapeseed (canola), sesame and groundnut (peanut) oils, plus coconut oil and palm oil.
Olives and avocados are fruits that supply lipid, which is unusual because most fruits contain almost none.
Nuts such as almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, peanuts and Brazil nuts are a concentrated source of lipid. So are seeds such as sunflower, sesame and flax (linseed).
Soya beans are a legume (a bean or pea crop) rich in both fat and protein.

Cereals and cereal products supply small amounts of lipid, mainly in wheat germ and oats. Wheat germ is the embryo of the wheat grain, the part that would grow into a new plant, so it holds the grain's fat.
Chocolate contains cocoa butter, which is the plant fat in cocoa.
Margarine and vegetable spreads are made from processed plant oils, so they count as vegetable sources. Shortening is another processed plant fat.
Vegetable oils are also hidden in biscuits, pastries, crisps, fried and takeaway foods and ready meals, which is why these foods are high in fat even though no oil is visible.
notes.tip: Name one clear plant food for each class, such as olive oil, sunflower oil, nuts, avocado, soya or margarine. Margarine and spreads are accepted as vegetable sources, so list them here as plant-based. Plant does not mean unsaturated, because coconut and palm oils are mostly saturated.

notes.b: Fish and other sea foods give a third group of lipid sources, quite different from the fat of land animals. How much fat a fish has, and where it keeps it, decides whether it counts as a rich source.
points: Oily fish such as salmon, mackerel, herring, sardines and trout store their fat in the flesh. They are a marine source of omega-3 fatty acids, a type of polyunsaturated fat, so the fat itself is the valuable part.
Fish-liver oils, such as cod-liver oil, provide polyunsaturated fat along with the fat-soluble vitamins A and D. Fish-oil supplements are another source of these.
White fish such as cod, haddock and whiting store their fat mainly in the liver, so the flesh is low in fat.
Shellfish, such as prawns and mussels, contain only small amounts of lipid.
notes.tip: Oily fish are animal foods but are classed as marine, so keep them in this group. Oily fish keep fat in the flesh, while white fish keep it in the liver and are low-fat. Oily fish are polyunsaturated and rich in omega-3, so name the benefit in one phrase.

notes.h: Distribution of saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fat in food (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Fats are made of fatty acids, which are saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated. Each food has a pattern in which one type is largest, and that pattern decides how healthy the fat is.
points: Mostly saturated fats are butter, cream, cheese, lard, suet, dripping, fat on meat and hard cooking fats. Animal fats such as these are generally saturated and associated with raised LDL (the blood cholesterol that harms arteries).
Coconut oil and palm oil are high in saturated fat despite coming from plants, so a food being a plant product does not make its fat unsaturated.
Olive oil, avocado and rapeseed (canola) oil are mostly monounsaturated, as are many nuts such as almonds, hazelnuts and peanuts.

Standard sunflower oil, corn oil and soya oil are mostly polyunsaturated, as are walnuts, seeds and oily fish. Plant and nut oils are associated with HDL, the blood cholesterol that protects the heart.
Sesame oil is a mixture of mono- and polyunsaturated fat, so it does not fit a single class.

Most foods contain all three fatty acid types, and a food is named for the type with the largest share. Butter, for example, contains a substantial share of monounsaturated fat as well as saturated fat, and olive oil contains some saturated fat.
The healthy swap is saturated fat for unsaturated fat, for example butter for olive oil.

Small amounts of naturally occurring trans fat appear in dairy and in beef and lamb fat. Industrial trans fat is limited in the EU to 2 g per 100 g of fat (Regulation (EU) 2019/649, applying from 1 April 2021).
notes.tip: Link each source to its type and its health effect: animal fats saturated and LDL-raising, olive oil monounsaturated, plant and nut oils polyunsaturated and HDL-associated. Animal does not always mean saturated, because oily fish contain much unsaturated fat, so keep oily fish in the marine group. Say standard sunflower oil if you state its class, because high-oleic sunflower oil is mostly monounsaturated.

notes.b: A poster turns the three groups of sources into a picture you can recall quickly in an exam. It works as revision rather than being examined itself.
points: Group the sources into three columns headed animal, vegetable (plant) and marine.
Give one example food for each column and the type of fatty acid that predominates in it.
Add the main health message for each food, such as the role of omega-3 in oily fish or the saturated fat in butter.
Show the source of each food with a small picture or label so the groups are clear at a glance.
notes.tip: Matching foods to their class is quick recall, so keep clean one-line lists for each column, such as avocado, sardines and cheese, or salmon, olive oil and butter.

questions.prompt: Name one lipid-rich food from each of the three source groups, animal, vegetable and marine, and state the main type of fatty acid in each.
questions.model: Animal: butter, with saturated fatty acids as the main type. Vegetable: olive oil, with monounsaturated fatty acids as the main type. Marine: oily fish such as mackerel, with polyunsaturated fatty acids as the main type, including omega-3. Award one mark for each correct food and one for each correct fatty acid type, up to 6.

questions.prompt: Sort a range of lipid-rich foods into animal, vegetable and marine sources, state which fatty acid type predominates in each, and explain which choices a household could make to lower its intake of saturated fat.
questions.model: Animal sources such as butter, lard, dripping and the fat in meat are mainly saturated. Vegetable sources such as olive oil and avocado are mainly monounsaturated; sunflower, corn and soya oils are mainly polyunsaturated. Marine sources such as oily fish are high in polyunsaturated fat, including omega-3. Coconut and palm oils come from plants but are high in saturated fat. To lower saturated fat, a household can replace butter, lard and fatty meat with vegetable oils, low-saturate spreads and oily fish, use lean cuts of meat and trim visible fat, and read labels to compare the saturated fat content of similar products.
